claim: Metabolic scaling refers to the inverse correlation of metabolic rates to body mass.
source: Metabolic scaling, the inverse correlation of metabolic rates to body mass, has been appreciated for more than 80 years.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a definition of metabolic scaling.

claim: Metabolic scaling has been appreciated for more than 80 years.
source: Metabolic scaling, the inverse correlation of metabolic rates to body mass, has been appreciated for more than 80 years.
evidence: This is a historical claim stated in the abstract.

claim: Studies of metabolic scaling have largely been restricted to mathematical modeling of caloric intake and oxygen consumption.
source: Studies of metabolic scaling have largely been restricted to mathematical modeling of caloric intake and oxygen consumption, and mostly rely on computational modeling.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior research stated in the abstract.

claim: The possibility that other metabolic processes scale with body size has not been comprehensively studied.
source: The possibility that other metabolic processes scale with body size has not been comprehensively studied.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Gene expression in livers of five species spanning a 30,000-fold range in mass revealed differential expression according to body mass of genes related to cytosolic and mitochondrial metabolic processes.
source: Gene expression in livers of five species spanning a 30,000-fold range in mass revealed differential expression according to body mass of genes related to cytosolic and mitochondrial metabolic processes, and to detoxication of oxidative damage.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomics data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Gene expression in livers of five species spanning a 30,000-fold range in mass revealed differential expression according to body mass of genes related to detoxication of oxidative damage.
source: Gene expression in livers of five species spanning a 30,000-fold range in mass revealed differential expression according to body mass of genes related to cytosolic and mitochondrial metabolic processes, and to detoxication of oxidative damage.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomics data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: While ordering of metabolic fluxes is not observed in in vitro cell-autonomous settings, it is present in liver slices and in vivo.
source: Comparing C57BL/6 J mice with Sprague-Dawley rats, we demonstrate that while ordering of metabolic fluxes is not observed in in vitro cell-autonomous settings, it is present in liver slices and in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Metabolic scaling is regulated at the level of gene and protein expression, enzyme activity, and substrate supply.
source: Together, these data reveal that metabolic scaling extends beyond oxygen consumption to other aspects of metabolism, and is regulated at the level of gene and protein expression, enzyme activity, and substrate supply.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple lines of evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: Max Kleiber published a seminal study on metabolic scaling in 1932.
source: In 1932, Max Kleiber published a seminal study (Kleiber, 1932), integrating prior reports demonstrating a phenomenon that came to be termed 'Kleiber's law,' or the principle of metabolic scaling.
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: Metabolic processes in many animals scale inversely to three-quarters of their body mass.
source: Metabolic scaling refers to the phenomenon that the metabolic processes in many animals, if not all, scale inversely to three-quarters of their body mass (West et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation.

claim: There is a reduction in metabolic rate as body size increases.
source: In simpler terms, there is a reduction in metabolic rate as body size increases.
evidence: This is a simplified explanation of metabolic scaling stated in the introduction.

claim: An elephant is 25 million times larger than a fruit fly, yet its energy expenditure is only 20 thousand times higher.
source: For example, an elephant is 25 million times larger than a fruit fly, yet its energy expenditure is only 20 thousand times higher; thus, from the fruit fly to elephant, the metabolic rate per gram of body weight scales down 1250 times.
evidence: This is an illustrative example provided in the introduction.

claim: From the fruit fly to elephant, the metabolic rate per gram of body weight scales down 1250 times.
source: For example, an elephant is 25 million times larger than a fruit fly, yet its energy expenditure is only 20 thousand times higher; thus, from the fruit fly to elephant, the metabolic rate per gram of body weight scales down 1250 times.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the example provided in the introduction.

claim: There is experimental evidence for metabolic scaling from bacteria to large mammals.
source: While there is experimental evidence for metabolic scaling from bacteria to large mammals, data have been generated almost exclusively from observations of caloric intake and oxygen consumption, with gene and protein expression, and substrate fluxes almost entirely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of prior research in the introduction.

claim: Prior metabolic scaling data have been generated almost exclusively from observations of caloric intake and oxygen consumption.
source: While there is experimental evidence for metabolic scaling from bacteria to large mammals, data have been generated almost exclusively from observations of caloric intake and oxygen consumption, with gene and protein expression, and substrate fluxes almost entirely unexplored.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior research stated in the introduction.

claim: Gene and protein expression, and substrate fluxes have been almost entirely unexplored in metabolic scaling studies.
source: While there is experimental evidence for metabolic scaling from bacteria to large mammals, data have been generated almost exclusively from observations of caloric intake and oxygen consumption, with gene and protein expression, and substrate fluxes almost entirely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in prior research in the introduction.

claim: The study examined liver gene expression across five species: mice, rats, monkeys, humans, and cattle.
source: Beginning at the transcriptional level, we studied liver gene expression across five species: mice (Mus musculus), rats (Rattus norvegicus), monkeys (Macaca mulatta), humans (Homo sapiens), and cattle (bos taurus), species with a 30,000-fold range of average body weight in adults (from 30 g in mice, to 900 kg in cattle).
evidence: This is a description of the study design stated in the introduction.

claim: The five species studied have a 30,000-fold range of average body weight in adults, from 30 g in mice to 900 kg in cattle.
source: Beginning at the transcriptional level, we studied liver gene expression across five species: mice (Mus musculus), rats (Rattus norvegicus), monkeys (Macaca mulatta), humans (Homo sapiens), and cattle (bos taurus), species with a 30,000-fold range of average body weight in adults (from 30 g in mice, to 900 kg in cattle).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the species studied.

claim: Numerous metabolic genes related to glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, oxygen consumption, electron transport, and redox function, and detoxification of oxidative damage, were expressed at levels inverse to body size.
source: Numerous metabolic genes related to glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, oxygen consumption, electron transport, and redox function, and detoxification of oxidative damage, were expressed at levels inverse to body size.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Approximately half of the genes in the liver that were expressed inversely proportionally to body size at the transcriptional level were also expressed at levels inversely proportional to body size at the level of protein expression.
source: Further analysis of liver proteomics revealed that approximately half of the genes in the liver that were expressed inversely proportionally to body size at the transcriptional level, were also expressed at levels inversely proportional to body size at the level of protein expression.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the introduction and supported by proteomics data in Figure 3.

claim: Rats exhibit lower metabolic rates when compared to mice in and ex vivo.
source: Our analysis shows that rats exhibit lower metabolic rates when compared to mice in and ex vivo; however, no significant differences were observed when we isolated hepatocytes and cultured them in vitro under identical conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: No significant differences in metabolic rates were observed between mice and rats when hepatocytes were isolated and cultured in vitro under identical conditions.
source: Our analysis shows that rats exhibit lower metabolic rates when compared to mice in and ex vivo; however, no significant differences were observed when we isolated hepatocytes and cultured them in vitro under identical conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Genes that are expressed inversely proportional to body weight in the liver are predominantly metabolic genes.
source: Genes within the liver that are expressed inversely proportional to body weight are predominantly metabolic genes
evidence: This is a section heading and primary finding supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: After normalizing for differences in transcript length and abundance across species, genes that followed the pattern of mouse >rat > monkey >human > cow were predominantly related to metabolic pathways, including pyruvate metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and glucose metabolism.
source: After normalizing for differences in transcript length and abundance across species, we filtered out genes that followed the pattern of mouse >rat > monkey >human > cow. The genes that met these criteria were predominantly related to metabolic pathways, including pyruvate metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and glucose metabolism (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results and supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Genes involved in amino acid, carbohydrate, energy, lipid, vitamin, and TCA cycle metabolism demonstrated a range of degrees of inverse correlation with body mass, with only TCA cycle genes clustering together.
source: Genes from this list were further restricted to genes involved in amino acid, carbohydrate, energy, lipid, vitamin, and TCA cycle metabolism, and demonstrated a range of degrees of inverse correlation with body mass, with only TCA cycle genes clustering together (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Eleven of sixteen critical metabolic enzymes that scaled required molecular oxygen, NAD+/NADH, or ATP/ADP for function.
source: Eleven of sixteen critical metabolic enzymes that scaled required molecular oxygen, NAD+/NADH, or ATP/ADP for function, possibly indicating exquisite regulation of energy-consuming processes at the individual gene level.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Genes involved in the detoxication of lipid peroxidation-derived aldehydes (ALDH7A1), hydrogen peroxide (GPX1), and ammonia (GLUL) suggest scaling of damage control mechanisms that are associated with increased oxidative metabolism across species.
source: Genes involved in the detoxication of lipid peroxidation-derived aldehydes (ALDH7A1), hydrogen peroxide (GPX1), and ammonia (GLUL) suggest scaling of damage control mechanisms that are associated with increased oxidative metabolism across species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings stated in the results and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The inverse correlation between body size and expression of genes that are associated with interorgan crosstalk is consistent with scaling in vivo which would not be expected in plated cells.
source: The inverse correlation between body size and expression of genes that are associated with interorgan crosstalk is consistent with scaling in vivo which would not be expected in plated cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings stated in the results.

claim: GPT1 is involved in recycling skeletal muscle-derived alanine back to liver-derived glucose.
source: For example, the differentially expressed genes include GPT1, which is involved in recycling skeletal muscle-derived alanine back to liver-derived glucose (Felig and Wahren, 1971; Petersen et al., 2019), and the adiponectin receptor (ADIPOR1), which binds an adipose tissue-derived hormone that regulates gluconeogenesis and fatty acid oxidation (Lin and Accili, 2011; Li et al., 2020 Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statement about gene function supported by citations.

claim: The adiponectin receptor (ADIPOR1) binds an adipose tissue-derived hormone that regulates gluconeogenesis and fatty acid oxidation.
source: For example, the differentially expressed genes include GPT1, which is involved in recycling skeletal muscle-derived alanine back to liver-derived glucose (Felig and Wahren, 1971; Petersen et al., 2019), and the adiponectin receptor (ADIPOR1), which binds an adipose tissue-derived hormone that regulates gluconeogenesis and fatty acid oxidation (Lin and Accili, 2011; Li et al., 2020 Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statement about gene function supported by citations.

claim: All three enzymes (Glul, Lipe, and Dlst) scaled relative to Actb.
source: We found that all three enzymes (Glul, Lipe, and Dlst) scaled relative to Actb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), whereas structural genes (collagenase 3 [Mmp3] and Larp1) did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that the differences in metabolic gene expression observed across species is likely not a result of global changes in RNA levels.
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Structural genes (collagenase 3 [Mmp3] and Larp1) did not scale relative to Actb.
source: We found that all three enzymes (Glul, Lipe, and Dlst) scaled relative to Actb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), whereas structural genes (collagenase 3 [Mmp3] and Larp1) did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that the differences in metabolic gene expression observed across species is likely not a result of global changes in RNA levels.
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: The differences in metabolic gene expression observed across species is likely not a result of global changes in RNA levels.
source: We found that all three enzymes (Glul, Lipe, and Dlst) scaled relative to Actb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), whereas structural genes (collagenase 3 [Mmp3] and Larp1) did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that the differences in metabolic gene expression observed across species is likely not a result of global changes in RNA levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the qPCR findings stated in the results.

claim: Three proteins (GLUL, GPX1, and MDH1) were found to follow a reverse correlation with body size.
source: The dataset contained protein expression corresponding to eight of the twenty genes identified to scale in our transcriptomics data analysis. Of these, three (GLUL, GPX1, and MDH1) were found to follow a reverse correlation with body size (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from proteomics analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 3A–C.

claim: GLUL protein was found to be expressed inversely proportionally to body size in the left ventricle of the heart.
source: Interestingly, one of these proteins (GLUL) was also found to be expressed inversely proportionally to body size in the left ventricle of the heart (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from proteomics analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Both alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) exhibited lower concentrations in humans as compared to rats and rats as compared to mice.
source: Additionally, we measured liver transaminase concentrations and observed that both alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) exhibited lower concentrations in humans as compared to rats and rats as compared to mice (Figure 3E–F), consistent with scaling at the level of protein expression as well as mRNA expression.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results and supported by Figure 3E–F.

claim: 30–40% lower activity of peroxidase and pyruvate carboxylase per mg tissue was observed in rats as compared to mice.
source: Finally, we utilized established enzymatic assays to measure the activity of peroxidase and pyruvate carboxylase in the livers of mice and rats. 30–40% lower activity of each enzyme per mg tissue was observed in rats as compared to mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting scaling at the level of metabolic enzyme activity.
evidence: This is a finding from enzymatic assays stated in the results and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: When PINTA was used to assess cytosolic and mitochondrial fluxes in plated hepatocytes, no significant differences were observed between species in any of the fluxes measured.
source: Consistent with the possibility that hepatocyte-extrinsic signals are primarily responsible for metabolic scaling, when we used PINTA to assess cytosolic and mitochondrial fluxes, we observed no significant differences between species in any of the fluxes measured in plated hepatocytes: glucose production, VPC, VCS, the contribution of glucose or fatty acids to the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, or lipolysis (Figure 4A–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro flux analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 4.

claim: A mitochondrial stress test in plated hepatocytes revealed no difference in any parameter between mice and rats.
source: Similarly, a mitochondrial stress test in plated hepatocytes revealed no difference in any parameter: neither basal mitochondrial and non-mitochondrial respiration, ATP production, maximal (uncoupled) respiration, spare respiratory capacity, nor proton leak differed between plated hepatocytes from mice and rats (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a finding from oxygen consumption analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 4I.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated scaling in vitro in cell suspensions only when analyzed immediately after hepatocyte isolation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated scaling in vitro in cell suspensions only when analyzed immediately after hepatocyte isolation (Porter and Brand, 1995), and have suggested that the phenomenon of scaling gradually disappears around 24 hr post removal (Brown et al., 2007), similar to the conditions in which we performed these studies.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citations.

claim: The phenomenon of scaling gradually disappears around 24 hr post removal from the organism.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated scaling in vitro in cell suspensions only when analyzed immediately after hepatocyte isolation (Porter and Brand, 1995), and have suggested that the phenomenon of scaling gradually disappears around 24 hr post removal (Brown et al., 2007), similar to the conditions in which we performed these studies.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citations.

claim: Most prior in vitro studies have demonstrated an absence of scaling, in contrast to in vivo.
source: Most prior in vitro studies have also demonstrated an absence of scaling, in contrast to in vivo (Glazier, 2015), and we extend these results to gluconeogenic and lipolytic fluxes in hepatocytes, glucose production in liver slices, and multimodal flux analysis in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citation.

claim: Liver glucose production per gram liver mass was threefold greater in mouse liver slices as compared to rats.
source: Indeed, we found that liver glucose production per gram liver mass was threefold greater in mouse liver slices as compared to rats (Figure 5A–B), suggesting that hepatocyte-extrinsic signals (for example, from other liver cell types) are involved in liver metabolic scaling.
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo liver slice studies stated in the results and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: Hepatocyte-extrinsic signals (for example, from other liver cell types) are involved in liver metabolic scaling.
source: Indeed, we found that liver glucose production per gram liver mass was threefold greater in mouse liver slices as compared to rats (Figure 5A–B), suggesting that hepatocyte-extrinsic signals (for example, from other liver cell types) are involved in liver metabolic scaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the liver slice findings stated in the results.

claim: Both endogenous glucose production and gluconeogenesis from pyruvate (VPC) per gram liver were more than twofold higher in mice than rats.
source: Using PINTA, we found that both endogenous glucose production and gluconeogenesis from pyruvate (VPC) per gram liver were more than twofold higher in mice than rats (Figure 6B–C), although the fractional contribution of pyruvate to gluconeogenesis did not differ between mice and rats (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo flux analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 6B–C.

claim: The fractional contribution of pyruvate to gluconeogenesis did not differ between mice and rats.
source: Using PINTA, we found that both endogenous glucose production and gluconeogenesis from pyruvate (VPC) per gram liver were more than twofold higher in mice than rats (Figure 6B–C), although the fractional contribution of pyruvate to gluconeogenesis did not differ between mice and rats (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo flux analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Mitochondrial oxidation scaled similarly, increasing threefold in mice as compared to rats studied under the same conditions.
source: Mitochondrial oxidation scaled similarly, increasing threefold in mice as compared to rats studied under the same conditions, due to increases in both glucose oxidation (pyruvate dehydrogenase flux, VPDH) and fatty acid oxidation (Figure 6D–F), associated with an increase in the ratio of pyruvate carboxylase anaplerosis to citrate synthase flux (VPC/VCS) without any difference in the fraction of VCS flux fueled by glucose through PDH (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo flux analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 6D–F.

claim: Whole-body fatty acid turnover, reflecting lipolysis, was 2.5-fold higher in mice than in rats.
source: These differences in metabolic fluxes according to body size applied not only to rodent liver metabolism but also to adipose tissue metabolism: whole-body fatty acid turnover, reflecting lipolysis, was 2.5-fold higher in mice than in rats (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo flux analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 6G.

claim: No sex differences were observed in any of the measured fluxes.
source: No sex differences were observed in any of the measured fluxes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1K–P).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1K–P.

claim: In vivo mitochondrial oxidation (TCA cycle flux) was threefold higher in mice than in rats, while in vitro measurements of oxygen consumption throughout a mitochondrial stress test, TCA cycle flux, and glucose production were not different between the species.
source: Taken together, these data emphasize the inadequacy of common in vitro methods as a readout of in vivo metabolism: whereas in vivo mitochondrial oxidation (TCA cycle flux) was threefold higher in mice than in rats, in vitro measurements of oxygen consumption throughout a mitochondrial stress test, TCA cycle flux, and glucose production were not different between the species (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a comparison of in vivo and in vitro findings stated in the results.

claim: The in vitro flux data showed no distinct clustering between species.
source: A clustering dendrogram was applied to our in vitro flux data and showed no distinct clustering between species (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from clustering analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 7B.

claim: The in vivo metabolic flux data led to distinct clustering of rats and mice.
source: However, the in vivo metabolic flux data led to distinct clustering of rats and mice (Figure 7C), providing a classical clustering-based objective analysis of in vitro versus in vivo metabolic flux.
evidence: This is a finding from clustering analysis stated in the results and supported by Figure 7C.

claim: Oxygen consumption has been shown to scale inversely with body mass in species ranging in mass across 20 orders of magnitude, from 10–14 to 106 grams.
source: Oxygen consumption has been shown to scale inversely with body mass in species ranging in mass across 20 orders of magnitude, from 10–14 to 106 grams (Ernest et al., 2003; Gillooly et al., 2001; Kleiber, 1932; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2008; Savage et al., 2004; West et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by multiple citations.

claim: Metabolic scaling has been shown to occur in prokaryotes.
source: This phenomenon has been most studied in mammals, but is highly conserved, having also been shown to occur in prokaryotes (Fenchel and Finlay, 1983; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2008; Moses et al., 2008), plants (Makarieva et al., 2005b; Mori et al., 2010; Reich et al., 2006), insects (Chown et al., 2007; Maino and Kearney, 2014; Makarieva et al., 2005a), fish (Clarke and Johnston, 1999; Gjoni et al., 2020; Rubalcaba et al., 2020), and birds (Glazier, 2008; Hudson et al., 2013; Makarieva et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citations.

claim: Metabolic scaling has been shown to occur in plants.
source: This phenomenon has been most studied in mammals, but is highly conserved, having also been shown to occur in prokaryotes (Fenchel and Finlay, 1983; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2008; Moses et al., 2008), plants (Makarieva et al., 2005b; Mori et al., 2010; Reich et al., 2006), insects (Chown et al., 2007; Maino and Kearney, 2014; Makarieva et al., 2005a), fish (Clarke and Johnston, 1999; Gjoni et al., 2020; Rubalcaba et al., 2020), and birds (Glazier, 2008; Hudson et al., 2013; Makarieva et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citations.

source: This phenomenon has been most studied in mammals, but is highly conserved, having also been shown to occur in prokaryotes (Fenchel and Finlay, 1983; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2008; Moses et al., 2008), plants (Makarieva et al., 2005b; Mori et al., 2010; Reich et al., 2006), insects (Chown et al., 2007; Maino and Kearney, 2014; Makarieva et al., 2005a), fish (Clarke and Johnston, 1999; Gjoni et al., 2020; Rubalcaba et al., 2020), and birds (Glazier, 2008; Hudson et al., 2013; Makarieva et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citations.

claim: Metabolic scaling has been shown to occur in fish.
source: This phenomenon has been most studied in mammals, but is highly conserved, having also been shown to occur in prokaryotes (Fenchel and Finlay, 1983; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2008; Moses et al., 2008), plants (Makarieva et al., 2005b; Mori et al., 2010; Reich et al., 2006), insects (Chown et al., 2007; Maino and Kearney, 2014; Makarieva et al., 2005a), fish (Clarke and Johnston, 1999; Gjoni et al., 2020; Rubalcaba et al., 2020), and birds (Glazier, 2008; Hudson et al., 2013; Makarieva et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citations.

claim: Metabolic scaling has been shown to occur in birds.
source: This phenomenon has been most studied in mammals, but is highly conserved, having also been shown to occur in prokaryotes (Fenchel and Finlay, 1983; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2005a; Makarieva et al., 2008; Moses et al., 2008), plants (Makarieva et al., 2005b; Mori et al., 2010; Reich et al., 2006), insects (Chown et al., 2007; Maino and Kearney, 2014; Makarieva et al., 2005a), fish (Clarke and Johnston, 1999; Gjoni et al., 2020; Rubalcaba et al., 2020), and birds (Glazier, 2008; Hudson et al., 2013; Makarieva et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citations.

claim: The metabolic processes observed to be higher in mice as compared to rats did not necessarily adhere quantitatively to the classic metabolic scaling relationship, with metabolic rates proportional to three-quarters of body mass.
source: It is important to note that the metabolic processes which we observed to be higher in mice as compared to rats did not necessarily adhere quantitatively to the classic metabolic scaling relationship, with metabolic rates proportional to three-quarters of body mass.
evidence: This is a caveat about the findings stated in the discussion.

claim: The scaling relationship is multidimensional: it is entirely conceivable that whole-body oxygen consumption could be proportional to three-quarters of body mass, while other metabolic processes may exhibit a different scaling relationship.
source: This speaks to the idea that the scaling relationship is multidimensional: it is entirely conceivable that whole-body oxygen consumption could be proportional to three-quarters of body mass, while other metabolic processes may exhibit a different scaling relationship.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion.

claim: The possibility that gene expression, as reflected by mRNA abundance, may also scale with body mass has not been previously addressed.
source: The possibility that gene expression, as reflected by mRNA abundance, may also scale with body mass has not been previously addressed.
evidence: This is a statement about novelty of the findings in the discussion.

claim: The collection of genes whose expression is inversely correlated with body mass is enriched for genes related to metabolic processes, and whose corresponding proteins' enzymatic action are constrained by the supply of substrate, NAD, ATP, or oxygen.
source: Rather, the collection of genes whose expression is inversely correlated with body mass is enriched for genes related to metabolic processes, and whose corresponding proteins' enzymatic action are constrained by the supply of substrate, NAD, ATP, or oxygen.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings stated in the discussion.

claim: Metabolic scaling cannot fully be explained at the transcriptional level, because many rate-limiting enzymes in the metabolic processes measured in vivo did not scale at the transcriptional level.
source: However, it should be noted that metabolic scaling cannot fully be explained at the transcriptional level, because many rate-limiting enzymes in the metabolic processes measured in vivo did not scale at the transcriptional level, and only approximately half of genes that scaled at the level of mRNA scaled at the level of protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings stated in the discussion.

claim: It is likely that both transcriptional and other mechanisms – such as enzyme activity – are responsible for variations in metabolic flux per unit mass, inversely proportionally to body size.
source: Thus, it is likely that both transcriptional and other mechanisms – such as enzyme activity – are responsible for variations in metabolic flux per unit mass, inversely proportionally to body size.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion.

claim: The currently available data do not allow us to assess whether the expression of certain isoforms of key metabolic enzymes scales differentially across species.
source: Additionally, the currently available data do not allow us to assess whether the expression of certain isoforms of key metabolic enzymes scales differentially across species.
evidence: This is a limitation stated in the discussion.

claim: Measurement of oxygen consumption in vitro may fail to detect any influence of scaling processes present in vivo.
source: Our findings emphasize that measurement of oxygen consumption in vitro may fail to detect any influence of scaling processes present in vivo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings stated in the discussion.

claim: Glucose production was threefold higher in mouse liver slices relative to rat liver slices, but did not significantly differ between plated hepatocytes from mice and rats.
source: Glucose production was threefold higher in mouse liver slices relative to rat liver slices, but did not significantly differ between plated hepatocytes from mice and rats.
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the discussion.

claim: The data do not allow us to ascertain whether differences in oxygen consumption orchestrate metabolic alterations, or metabolic alterations require changes in oxygen consumption.
source: For example, our data do not allow us to ascertain whether differences in oxygen consumption orchestrate metabolic alterations, as has been suggested in the setting of cancer cells (Nakazawa et al., 2016), or metabolic alterations require changes in oxygen consumption.
evidence: This is a limitation stated in the discussion.

claim: There are limitations to the fact that metabolic flux studies were performed only in the two arguably most related species included in the transcriptomics analysis.
source: Additionally, there are limitations to the fact that metabolic flux studies were performed only in the two arguably most related species included in the transcriptomics analysis (with monkey and human perhaps being similarly related).
evidence: This is a limitation stated in the discussion.

claim: Experimental and computational data suggest that the metabolic scaling relationship with regard to oxygen consumption holds at least from birds to cattle.
source: However, experimental and computational data suggest that the metabolic scaling relationship with regard to oxygen consumption holds at least from birds to cattle, and that a similar – but not identical – scaling relationship exists in plants (Niklas and Kutschera, 2015), so we posit that it is likely that if such a threshold exists, it occurs at a body size orders of magnitude larger than the rodents included in our study.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citation.

claim: A similar – but not identical – scaling relationship exists in plants.
source: However, experimental and computational data suggest that the metabolic scaling relationship with regard to oxygen consumption holds at least from birds to cattle, and that a similar – but not identical – scaling relationship exists in plants (Niklas and Kutschera, 2015), so we posit that it is likely that if such a threshold exists, it occurs at a body size orders of magnitude larger than the rodents included in our study.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research supported by citation.

claim: The phenomenon of metabolic scaling extends to processes beyond oxygen consumption and caloric intake, and is bookended by scaling not only of gene and protein expression, but also of enzyme activity and cytosolic and mitochondrial fluxes in vivo.
source: Taken together, the findings of this study show that the phenomenon of metabolic scaling extends to processes beyond oxygen consumption and caloric intake, and is bookended by scaling not only of gene and protein expression, but also of enzyme activity and cytosolic and mitochondrial fluxes in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: If one were to alter the activity of an enzyme in a larger species using a mutation to increase it to the level of activity of the same enzyme in a smaller species, the phenomenon of metabolic scaling might disappear.
source: It may be that if one were to alter the activity of an enzyme in a larger species using a mutation to increase it to the level of activity of the same enzyme in a smaller species, that the phenomenon of metabolic scaling might disappear.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the discussion.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the phenomenon of metabolic scaling remain obscure, and deserve investigation as a fundamental question in biology.
source: The mechanisms underlying the phenomenon of metabolic scaling remain obscure, and deserve investigation as a fundamental question in biology (Hatton et al., 2019; Kolokotrones et al., 2010; White and Seymour, 2003).
